title: The AI trade is unraveling again as chips, neoclouds, and hyperscalers drop
byline: Huileng Tan, Theron Mohamed, Jennifer Sor
excerpt: Nvidia stock plunged and Anthropic continued its post-IPO slide. The AI trade has been hugely volatile, with chip stocks and neoclouds getting crushed.
content_html:
The AI trade is swinging wildly days after Jensen Huang's comeback sparked a huge rally

By Huileng Tan

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

, Theron Mohamed

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

,and Jennifer Sor

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-25T21:06:10.358Z

It was a wild day for the AI trade ahead of Thanksgiving.

Just days after a parabolic rally sparked by Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, US stocks were mostly lower again, falling sharply in early trading but managing to pare the deepest losses by the closing bell.

The Nasdaq 100 fell as much as 4%, and the S&P 500 fell as much as 3%, with both ending the session down less than 1%.

The huge swings attests to how temperamental the AI trade has become, with big events like Huang's return and the Anthropic IPO unable to lift sentiment and restart the bull rally. Chips, neoclouds, and hyperscalers were all down sharply on Wednesday. Nvidia dropped as much as 9%, and remains down more than 30% from its early October high.

Anthropic, however, made a remarkable round-trip move during the session, dropping as much as 10% in the morning before turning positive in afternoon trading. Shares of the Claude maker popped back above the IPO price of $83 before ending slightly below that threshold at $82.79

Dell, notably, dropped as much as 8% before closing slightly higher. The PC hardware maker saw intense volatility despite reported blockbuster results for the third quarter after the bell on Tuesday.

"Dell just put up one of the best quarters of the AI cycle, and the stock barely moved, yet another sign that the market is 'over' the AI trade," Luke Lango, an independent tech analyst, wrote in a note. "That's the AI transition period in a nutshell: the fundamentals are booming, but the market is pricing in a slowdown that hasn't shown up in the numbers yet."

Here's where US indexes stood at the 4:00 p.m. ET closing bell:

  • S&P 500: 7,183.08, down 0.25%
  • Dow Jones Industrial Average: 50,189.08, up 0.34% (+170.38 points)
  • Nasdaq 100: 26,050.15, down 0.63%

Here were the most notable moves in the tech sector:

Meanwhile, hot inflation data and the prospect of additional tariffs from the Trump administration were adding to the selling pressure.

Analysts had been mulling whether Monday's relief rally was a dead-cat bounce, a short-lived recovery in stocks before the market makes its way to a new low.

A few worries appear to have triggered the latest bout of selling:

  • Doubts have been swirling around Nvidia's future, given the ongoing investigation into Huang and uncertainty that continues to loom over the firm's future financing deals and business in China.

    "Perception is important, and the current perception of Nvidia's board is not the one that the world's leading chip designer should want," David Morrison, a senior market analyst at Trade Nation, said about Huang's reinstatement in a client note.

    Huang is scheduled to testify before the US Senate Banking Committee on December 3 about US chip-export controls, amid mounting congressional scrutiny of Nvidia.

    Huang's reinstatement has not removed the political uncertainty surrounding AI, Macquarie Group strategists warned.

    "That's because with Huang at Nvidia or not, it's safe to say that the politicians are still 'coming after' AI," they wrote.

  • Investors are growing anxious that the AI boom is starting to crumble. The market has pent-up anxiety about the trajectory of capex spending, and any hint that firms are either spending too little or too much on AI has triggered a wave of panic-selling recently.

    "There is a sense of caution on the markets, with investors not quite sure if they should go all-in on tech again, or whether Monday's Nvidia-fuelled tech rally was a one-day affair," Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said in a morning note.

  • The short trading week is likely prompting some of the volatility, as more traders step away from the markets for the holidays. The result can be less liquidity, which can exaggerate moves in either direction, Mark Newton, the head of technical strategy at Fundstrat Research, said.
  • New core inflation data came in hotter-than-expected. Core personal consumption expenditures, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, accelerated to a 3.3% yearly pace in October. Markets are now almost certain the Fed will hike rates in December, pricing in a 99.8% probability that a 25-basis-point increase is coming before year-end, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

  • The prospect of additional tariffs is rattling investors. Reports circulated this week that the Trump administration is readying to unveil a new slate of levies on China and other trading partners this week. It also puts the spotlight on inflation and the likelihood that rates will move higher, a headwind for stocks.

    "The threat of another wave of tariffs by Donald Trump could cause unease, particularly if they are seen to cause new inflationary pressures," Coatsworth added, referring to news reports that the Trump administration is preparing to impose fresh taxes on imports from China and other trading partners.

Wall Street is eyeing the possibility that selling will continue for the foreseeable future.

JPMorgan analysts said they were flipping from a tactically bullish to a "Tactically Cautious" view on stocks, pointing to uncertainty around Nvidia in particular.

"In hindsight, it seems obvious that we should have been on the sidelines but we, similar to the market, had viewed NVDA and capital markets activity as the necessary support for Tech to form a bottom and thus whiffed on the tactical bullish call," the bank's market intelligence team wrote in a client note. "Now, the uncertainty surrounding NVDA and peers and opacity over 2028 and beyond makes Tech longs highly uncertain in the very near-term."

Fundstrat's Newton said near-term market trends looked "negative." He said he was searching for signs that tech stocks were starting to gain an edge over defensives, which could happen in the next two weeks, due to seasonal patterns in the market.

"Until that leadership starts to roll over, it's difficult to have conviction that risk appetite has returned in a meaningful way," he said.

content_html_zh:
The AI trade is swinging wildly days after Jensen Huang's comeback sparked a huge rally

作者：Huileng Tan 您目前正在关注该作者！ Click to unsubscribe from email alerts. , Theron Mohamed You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts. ,and Jennifer Sor You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-25T21:06:10.358Z

It was a wild day for the AI trade ahead of Thanksgiving.

Just days after a parabolic rally sparked by Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, US stocks were mostly lower again, falling sharply in early trading but managing to pare the deepest losses by the closing bell.

The Nasdaq 100 fell as much as 4%, and the S&P 500 fell as much as 3%, with both ending the session down less than 1%.

The huge swings attests to how temperamental the AI trade has become, with big events like Huang's return and the Anthropic IPO unable to lift sentiment and restart the bull rally. Chips, neoclouds, and hyperscalers were all down sharply on Wednesday. Nvidia dropped as much as 9%, and remains down more than 30% from its early October high.

Anthropic, however, made a remarkable round-trip move during the session, dropping as much as 10% in the morning before turning positive in afternoon trading. Shares of the Claude maker popped back above the IPO price of $83 before ending slightly below that threshold at $82.79

Dell, notably, dropped as much as 8% before closing slightly higher. The PC hardware maker saw intense volatility despite reported blockbuster results for the third quarter after the bell on Tuesday.

"Dell just put up one of the best quarters of the AI cycle, and the stock barely moved, yet another sign that the market is 'over' the AI trade," Luke Lango, an independent tech analyst, wrote in a note. "That's the AI transition period in a nutshell: the fundamentals are booming, but the market is pricing in a slowdown that hasn't shown up in the numbers yet."

Here's where US indexes stood at the 4:00 p.m. 东部时间收盘钟声：

  • S&P 500: 7,183.08, down 0.25%
  • Dow Jones Industrial Average: 50,189.08, up 0.34% (+170.38 points)
  • Nasdaq 100: 26,050.15, down 0.63%

Here were the most notable moves in the tech sector:

SandiskSNDK-22%

MetaMETA+3%

Meanwhile, hot inflation data and the prospect of additional tariffs from the Trump administration were adding to the selling pressure.

Analysts had been mulling whether Monday's relief rally was a dead-cat bounce, a short-lived recovery in stocks before the market makes its way to a new low.

A few worries appear to have triggered the latest bout of selling:

  • Doubts have been swirling around Nvidia's future, given the ongoing investigation into Huang and uncertainty that continues to loom over the firm's future financing deals and business in China."Perception is important, and the current perception of Nvidia's board is not the one that the world's leading chip designer should want," David Morrison, a senior market analyst at Trade Nation, said about Huang's reinstatement in a client note.Huang is scheduled to testify before the US Senate Banking Committee on December 3 about US chip-export controls, amid mounting congressional scrutiny of Nvidia.Huang's reinstatement has not removed the political uncertainty surrounding AI, Macquarie Group strategists warned."That's because with Huang at Nvidia or not, it's safe to say that the politicians are still 'coming after' AI," they wrote.
  • Investors are growing anxious that the AI boom is starting to crumble. The market has pent-up anxiety about the trajectory of capex spending, and any hint that firms are either spending too little or too much on AI has triggered a wave of panic-selling recently."There is a sense of caution on the markets, with investors not quite sure if they should go all-in on tech again, or whether Monday's Nvidia-fuelled tech rally was a one-day affair," Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said in a morning note.
  • The short trading week is likely prompting some of the volatility, as more traders step away from the markets for the holidays. The result can be less liquidity, which can exaggerate moves in either direction, Mark Newton, the head of technical strategy at Fundstrat Research, said.
  • New core inflation data came in hotter-than-expected. Core personal consumption expenditures, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, accelerated to a 3.3% yearly pace in October. Markets are now almost certain the Fed will hike rates in December, pricing in a 99.8% probability that a 25-basis-point increase is coming before year-end, according to the CME FedWatch tool.
  • The prospect of additional tariffs is rattling investors. Reports circulated this week that the Trump administration is readying to unveil a new slate of levies on China and other trading partners this week. It also puts the spotlight on inflation and the likelihood that rates will move higher, a headwind for stocks."The threat of another wave of tariffs by Donald Trump could cause unease, particularly if they are seen to cause new inflationary pressures," Coatsworth added, referring to news reports that the Trump administration is preparing to impose fresh taxes on imports from China and other trading partners.

Wall Street is eyeing the possibility that selling will continue for the foreseeable future.

JPMorgan analysts said they were flipping from a tactically bullish to a "Tactically Cautious" view on stocks, pointing to uncertainty around Nvidia in particular.

"In hindsight, it seems obvious that we should have been on the sidelines but we, similar to the market, had viewed NVDA and capital markets activity as the necessary support for Tech to form a bottom and thus whiffed on the tactical bullish call," the bank's market intelligence team wrote in a client note. "Now, the uncertainty surrounding NVDA and peers and opacity over 2028 and beyond makes Tech longs highly uncertain in the very near-term."

Fundstrat's Newton said near-term market trends looked "negative." He said he was searching for signs that tech stocks were starting to gain an edge over defensives, which could happen in the next two weeks, due to seasonal patterns in the market.

"Until that leadership starts to roll over, it's difficult to have conviction that risk appetite has returned in a meaningful way," he said.
